title: Brain and Subjective Responses to Indoor Environments Related to Concentration and Creativity
research_question: How do brainwave responses associated with concentration and creativity vary with changes in interior design elements (shape, furniture arrangement, ceiling height, color, and view of nature)? How do they differ by EEG channel? For which stimuli are the brainwaves significantly different from those of the prestimulation? Overall, which interior design elements tend to activate brainwaves relevant to concentration and creativity? According to participants' subjective responses, which stimuli do they believe will help them focus, and which will help them think creatively? How similar or different are the brain's responses and the subjective responses?

participants.description: 14 females (67%) and 6 males (33%), age range 18–29 years (average 22.7 years). 12 majored in housing design-related fields, 8 in other majors. No visual or color perception problems.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through an announcement sent to people on the mailing list of Kyung Hee University college.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 19 images of classroom environments (14 x 8.3 m) created using SketchUp and Enscape. 16 images combined four elements: space shape (curvilinear/rectilinear), furniture arrangement (collaborative/traditional), ceiling height (4m/2.7m), and wall color (deep blue 8.7B 4/5 / deep red 2.5R 4/8). 3 additional images: common white wall, full-window wall with natural scenery, and a blue wall without windows. A gray screen (Ref2) was used as a pre-stimulus baseline.

measures.instrument: (SMR + mβ)/θ, derived from EEG signals (12-15 Hz SMR, 15-20 Hz mid-beta, 4-8 Hz theta)
Relative theta wave activity (4-8 Hz theta band power relative to total power), derived from EEG signals
Self-report question: 'Which stimulus would help you best concentrate?' (forced choice)
Self-report question: 'Which stimulus would help you best think creatively?' (forced choice)

findings.antecedent: Rectilinear space shape (A16) under traditional furniture arrangement, low ceiling height, and red color
findings.mechanism: Rectilinear forms and traditional arrangements may create a relatively tense environment, increasing CI.
findings.quote: higher CI values were observed in rectilinear forms (A16) compared to curvilinear forms (A1).

findings.antecedent: Traditional furniture arrangement (A15) under rectilinear forms, high ceiling height, and red color
findings.mechanism: Traditional arrangements may help maintain attention on the teacher.
findings.quote: Higher CI values were also observed in the traditional furniture arrangement (A15) compared to the collaborative furniture arrangement (A10).

findings.antecedent: Red wall color (A2) under curvilinear forms, collaborative arrangement, and low ceiling height
findings.mechanism: Red color is known to evoke attention and signify alertness.
findings.quote: red (A2) showed a higher CI than blue (A6).

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear space shape (A1) under traditional furniture arrangement, high ceiling height, and blue color
findings.mechanism: Curvilinear forms evoke more pleasant emotions, which facilitate creative problem-solving.
findings.quote: Higher RT values were found in curvilinear forms (A1, A2, A3, and A4)

findings.antecedent: Collaborative furniture arrangement (A10) under rectilinear forms, high ceiling height, and blue color
findings.mechanism: Collaborative arrangements are associated with a gentle atmosphere conducive to teamwork and communication.
findings.quote: collaborative arrangements of furniture layouts (A10 and A11) showed higher RT.

findings.antecedent: White wall (A17) classroom environment
findings.mechanism: Participants perceived white walls as best for concentration.
findings.quote: selected the classroom with the white wall most often (S17, 45%)

findings.antecedent: Traditional front-facing linear furniture layout
findings.mechanism: Traditional layouts help maintain students' attention to the teacher.
findings.quote: A common feature is a traditional front-facing linear furniture layout.

findings.antecedent: Full nature view (A18) classroom environment
findings.mechanism: Natural elements are beneficial for concentration and creativity.
findings.quote: participants selected S18 (full nature view, 45%)

findings.antecedent: Collaborative furniture layout
findings.mechanism: Collaborative layouts encourage face-to-face interactions and benefit creativity.
findings.quote: The common features were the collaborative furniture layout and curvilinear shape.

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear space shape
findings.mechanism: Curvilinear forms evoke more pleasant emotions, which facilitate creative problem-solving.
findings.quote: The common features were the collaborative furniture layout and curvilinear shape.

findings.antecedent: Blue walls (A13) compared to white walls (A17)
findings.mechanism: Blue walls may induce higher CI values than white walls.
findings.quote: Higher CI values were observed for these stimuli than for A17

findings.antecedent: Red walls (A16) compared to white walls (A17)
findings.mechanism: Red walls may induce higher CI values than white walls.
findings.quote: the most significant differences observed in A16, which had red walls.

findings.antecedent: Blue walls (A13) compared to white walls (A17)
findings.mechanism: White walls may produce higher RT values than blue walls.
findings.quote: A13 (blue) and A16 (red) ... exhibited lower RT values than A17.

findings.antecedent: Red walls (A16) compared to white walls (A17)
findings.mechanism: White walls may produce higher RT values than red walls.
findings.quote: white walls produced the highest RT values, followed by blue and red walls.

findings.antecedent: Red walls (A16) compared to full nature view (A18)
findings.mechanism: Red walls tend to have higher concentration than nature views.
findings.quote: CI was significantly higher in A16 than in A18.

findings.antecedent: Full nature view (A18) compared to red walls (A16)
findings.mechanism: Nature views tend to have higher creativity than red walls.
findings.quote: RT was significantly higher in A18 than in A16.

findings.antecedent: Most stimuli (A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7, A8, A11, A12, A14, A15, A16, A17, A18, A19) compared to gray screen (Ref2)
findings.mechanism: The gray screen (Ref2) served as a neutral baseline without stimulation, suggesting that the stimuli themselves might have introduced cognitive load or distraction.
findings.quote: the CI was significantly lower in some channels in most stimuli than in Ref2, suggesting a decrease in concentration after the stimulus

findings.antecedent: Most stimuli (A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7, A8, A13, A14, A15, A17, A18, A19) compared to gray screen (Ref2)
findings.mechanism: Theta waves are associated with creative problem-solving and insight, suggesting the stimuli activated creativity-related brain activity.
findings.quote: RT was significantly higher in some channels of most stimuli than in Ref2, suggesting an increase in creativity after the stimulus

findings.antecedent: Indoor environmental elements (shape, furniture arrangement, ceiling height, color, view of nature)
findings.mechanism: Different elements activate different brain regions and cognitive processes related to concentration and creativity.
findings.quote: CI and RT values showed opposite tendencies in the left and right hemispheres.

findings.antecedent: Rectilinear forms, traditional furniture arrangements, and red color
findings.mechanism: These elements may create a more structured or alerting environment, conducive to focused attention.
findings.quote: the closely associated features were red, rectilinear shapes, and traditional furniture arrangements.

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear shapes, collaborative furniture arrangements, and walls made entirely of glass (natural scenery)
findings.mechanism: These elements may foster a sense of uniqueness, pleasantness, and social interaction, promoting creative thinking.
findings.quote: the closely associated features were curvilinear shapes, collaborative furniture arrangements, and walls made entirely of glass

findings.antecedent: Traditional furniture layout
findings.consequent: Concentration (both brain CI and subjective response)
findings.mechanism: Traditional layouts help maintain students' attention to the teacher.
findings.quote: responses to front-facing furniture layout were associated with concentration, while a view of nature

findings.antecedent: View of nature, collaborative furniture layout, and curvilinear shape
findings.consequent: Creativity (both brain RT and subjective response)
findings.mechanism: These elements foster a sense of uniqueness, pleasantness, and social interaction, promoting creative thinking.
findings.quote: a view of nature, collaborative furniture layout, and curvilinear shape were associated with creativity aligned.

findings.antecedent: Color (red/blue vs white)
findings.mechanism: Discrepancy between immediate brain response and conscious preference.
findings.quote: Responses to color, however, differed.

findings.antecedent: Stimuli (classroom images)
findings.mechanism: Visual stimuli induce brainwave activity, with different elements affecting different cognitive states.
findings.quote: participants' brainwaves in response to the stimuli in this study were observed more frequently in the parietal (P3, P4) and occipital lobes (O1, O2)

findings.antecedent: Right hemisphere (Fp, F, P lobes)
findings.mechanism: The right brain plays a leading role in attention allocation.
findings.quote: the values of Fp, F, and P were slightly higher on the right than on the left.

findings.antecedent: Left hemisphere (Fp, P, O lobes)
findings.mechanism: The left hemisphere theta wave PSD value is higher than that of the right hemisphere, potentially linked to creative thinking.
findings.quote: the values in Fp, P, and O were higher on the left side than on the right.

mechanisms: Rectilinear forms and traditional arrangements may create a relatively tense environment, increasing CI.
Curvilinear forms evoke more pleasant emotions, which facilitate creative problem-solving.
Collaborative arrangements are associated with a gentle atmosphere conducive to teamwork and communication, promoting creativity.
Red color is known to evoke attention and signify alertness, increasing CI.
Natural elements (views of nature) are beneficial for concentration and creativity.
White walls may produce higher RT values, followed by blue and red walls.
The right brain plays a leading role in attention allocation (higher CI on right Fp, F, P).
The left hemisphere theta wave PSD value is higher than that of the right hemisphere (higher RT on left Fp, P, O), potentially linked to creative thinking.
Concentration and creativity have contrasting characteristics, thus indoor environments optimized for each will likely have some degree of contrasting characteristics.
implementation_implications: Furniture arrangements and color are affordable recommendations for achieving desired learning effects due to their mobility and ease of alteration.
Curvilinear forms should be considered for walls, lighting fixtures, furniture shapes, or other classroom objects to enhance creativity.
Prioritize frontal furniture arrangement for concentration and collaborative arrangement, curved shapes, and natural views for creativity in educational spaces.
Incorporate biophilic design into breakout areas inside and outside classrooms to encourage creativity and recreation.
Organize spaces with different characteristics within a school or educational space to allow selection based on educational goals.

limitations: Used rendered images instead of real environments, which may differ in experience.
Used a monitor instead of VR head-mounted display due to discomfort and potential brainwave interference.
Small number of participants (N=20) limits generalization of results.
Did not measure specific tasks involving concentration and creativity, so it's uncertain if people actually perform better in classrooms with revealed stimuli characteristics.
Scale ratings for subjective responses were not available for all stimuli, preventing within-subject correlation analysis.

paper_metadata.title: Brain and Subjective Responses to Indoor Environments Related to Concentration and Creativity
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Brain and Subjective Responses to Indoor Environments Related to Concentration and Creativity
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Electroencephalograms (EEGs) can be used to study the influence of environmental elements on human emotions, cognition, and behavior. EEGs can reveal unconscious responses and fill in the gaps left by subjective responses provided in survey questionnaires or interviews. EEG research on the impact of classroom design elements on concentration and creativity is scarce; the design elements studied have not been diverse enough. In addition, no researchers have examined the brain and subjective responses to multiple indoor environmental elements regarding concentration and creativity. Thus, the purpose of this study was to explore how the human brain responds to different indoor environmental elements as shown by objective EEG signals related to concentration and creativity, and their similarities and differences to subjective self-reported responses. The experimental stimuli included 16 images combining four indoor environmental elements—classroom space shape, furniture arrangement, ceiling height, and color—along with images of white walls, a full-window wall with a view of nature, and a windowless scenario, totaling 19 images. The brainwaves of 20 people collected from eight channels were analyzed to determine the concentration index (CI) for concentration and relative theta (RT) for creativity. As a subjective response, participants were asked to choose the stimuli in which they felt they could best concentrate and be most creative in a self-report format. The results showed the following tendencies: (a) More brainwaves in the parietal and occipital lobes than in the prefrontal or frontal lobes; (b) a higher CI with rectilinear shapes, traditional frontal furniture arrangements, and red walls; (c) a higher RT with curvilinear shapes, collaborative furniture arrangements, white walls, and a full view of nature; and (d) participants selected white walls and a front-facing furniture layout as supportive of concentration and a full view of nature, curvilinear shape, and collaborative furniture layout for creative thinking. The results showed that similarities in brain and subjective responses were related to furniture layout and shape, whereas differences existed in color. This study contributes to the understanding of the characteristics of indoor environments that appear to enhance the manifestation of concentration and creativity.
